prompts: I'm using Python. What does weave.init do, and what project string should I pass?

output.answer:
**What it does:** `weave.init()` initializes Weave for your project so tracing works. In the agent workflow it authenticates with Weights & Biases and configures the OTel exporter that sends agent spans to the **Agents** view [S1]. It also registers your team and project so the SDK routes spans to the right place in the UI [S2]. If the project doesn't exist on your team, Weave creates it the first time you write to it [S1]. Call it before any agent tracing calls such as `start_conversation()` or `start_turn()`. Without it, those functions silently do nothing [S2].

**What to pass in Python:** the recommended form is a `"team/project"` string:

```python
import weave
weave.init("[YOUR-TEAM]/[YOUR-PROJECT]")
```

- `[YOUR-TEAM]` is your CoreWeave Forge team name.
- `[YOUR-PROJECT]` is your Weights & Biases project name [S2].

You can also build the string, for example `weave.init(f"{TEAM}/{PROJECT}")` [S1].

**Bare project name:** other Python examples pass only a project name, such as `weave.init("langchain_demo")`. The LangChain page says this argument is a project name Weave uses to organize your traces [S4]. The TypeScript reference says the argument can be `project` or `entity/project`. If you omit the team, your default entity is used [S3]. I didn't find a Python reference page for `weave.init` in the snapshot, so I can't confirm that the Python default-entity behavior is identical. To avoid ambiguity, pass `team/project` explicitly.

**Next step:** put `weave.init("your-team/your-project")` near the top of your script, before you create any traces. Make sure `WANDB_API_KEY` is set in your environment. The quickstart does this before calling `weave.init` [S1].

# Trace your agents

> Use the Weave SDK to instrument multi-turn agentic applications and view them in the Agents tab.

> [!TIP]
>
> **This workflow is also available in CoreWeave Agent Lens.** Agent Lens is the Forge experience built for tracing, monitoring, and analyzing AI agents, with automated insights into agent failures and user intents. It uses the same trace data as Weights & Biases Weave, so the traces you already send appear there with nothing to migrate.
> [See how to do this in Agent Lens](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/agent-lens/tracing/instrument.md).

Learn how to instrument a multi-turn agentic application using the W\&B Weave SDK so that you can view, debug, and evaluate your agent's behavior. This guide is intended for developers who build or integrate agents and want structured visibility into conversations, turns, LLM calls, and tool executions.

The Weave SDK for Agents models the full lifecycle of a multi-turn agent conversation: the agent that owns many conversations, the conversation that groups turns together, each user-agent exchange (turn), the LLM calls within a turn, and the tool executions that an LLM triggers. Traces appear in the **Agents** tab of your Weave project. Each conversation shows a multi-turn timeline with nested tool calls, token usage, and feedback.

Weave is built on [OpenTelemetry (OTel)](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/), the open standard for distributed tracing. Every turn, LLM call, and tool call emits an OTel *span* (a structured record of one operation). Each span is tagged with [GenAI semantic-convention](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/gen-ai/) attributes like `gen_ai.agent.name` and `gen_ai.conversation.id`.

If you're tracing individual functions as Ops with the `@weave.op` decorator, see [Trace LLM applications](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/tracing.md) instead.

# LangChain

> Use Weave to track and log all calls made through the LangChain Python library

[Try in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/github/wandb/examples/blob/master/weave/docs/quickstart_langchain.ipynb)

Weave tracks and logs calls made through the [LangChain Python library](https://github.com/langchain-ai/langchain).

When working with LLMs, debugging is part of the job. Whether a model call fails, an output is misformatted, or nested model calls create confusion, pinpointing issues can be hard. LangChain applications often consist of multiple steps and LLM call invocations, so it helps to understand the inner workings of your chains and agents.

Weave captures traces for your [LangChain](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langchain/overview) applications automatically. This lets you monitor and analyze your application's performance, which makes it easier to debug and optimize your LLM workflows.

This guide is for developers building LangChain applications who want to add tracing, evaluation, and observability with Weave. It walks through enabling automatic tracing, attaching metadata, controlling tracing manually, and wrapping LangChain chains as Weave models for evaluation.

## Publish an object

Weave's serialization layer saves and versions objects.

**Python**

```python lines theme={"system"}
import weave
weave.init("your-team-name/your-project-name")
# Save a list, giving it the name 'cat-names'
weave.publish(['felix', 'jimbo', 'billie'], 'cat-names')
```

**TypeScript**

TypeScript publishing support is limited. Not all objects are supported.

```typescript twoslash lines theme={"system"}
// @noErrors
import * as weave from 'weave'

const client = await weave.init("your-team-name/your-project-name")

// Save an array, giving it the name 'cat-names'
client.publish(['felix', 'jimbo', 'billie'], 'cat-names')
```

When you save an object with a name, Weave creates the first version of that object if it doesn't exist.

To deep-link from your own UI to a conversation in the Weave Agents view, build the URL from your entity, project, and the conversation id. `weave.init()` returns a client that carries `entity` and `project`, and `start_conversation` exposes `conversation_id`.

from weave.trace.urls import agent_conversation_path

client = weave.init(f"{TEAM}/{PROJECT}")

    # ... run turns ...
    url = agent_conversation_path(
        client.entity, client.project, conversation.conversation_id
    )
    print(f"View this conversation at {url}")
```

# Trace your agents

> Use the Weave SDK to instrument multi-turn agentic applications and view them in the Agents tab.

> [!TIP]
>
> **This workflow is also available in CoreWeave Agent Lens.** Agent Lens is the Forge experience built for tracing, monitoring, and analyzing AI agents, with automated insights into agent failures and user intents. It uses the same trace data as Weights & Biases Weave, so the traces you already send appear there with nothing to migrate.
> [See how to do this in Agent Lens](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/agent-lens/tracing/instrument.md).

Learn how to instrument a multi-turn agentic application using the W\&B Weave SDK so that you can view, debug, and evaluate your agent's behavior. This guide is intended for developers who build or integrate agents and want structured visibility into conversations, turns, LLM calls, and tool executions.

The Weave SDK for Agents models the full lifecycle of a multi-turn agent conversation: the agent that owns many conversations, the conversation that groups turns together, each user-agent exchange (turn), the LLM calls within a turn, and the tool executions that an LLM triggers. Traces appear in the **Agents** tab of your Weave project. Each conversation shows a multi-turn timeline with nested tool calls, token usage, and feedback.

Weave is built on [OpenTelemetry (OTel)](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/), the open standard for distributed tracing. Every turn, LLM call, and tool call emits an OTel *span* (a structured record of one operation). Each span is tagged with [GenAI semantic-convention](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/gen-ai/) attributes like `gen_ai.agent.name` and `gen_ai.conversation.id`.

If you're tracing individual functions as Ops with the `@weave.op` decorator, see [Trace LLM applications](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/tracing.md) instead.

When working with LLMs, debugging is part of the job. Whether a model call fails, an output is misformatted, or nested model calls create confusion, pinpointing issues can be hard. **What it does:** `weave.init()` initializes Weave for your project so tracing works. In the agent workflow it authenticates with Weights & Biases and configures the OTel exporter that sends agent spans to the **Agents** view [S1]. It also registers your team and project so the SDK routes spans to the right place in the UI [S2]. If the project doesn't exist on your team, Weave creates it the first time you write to it [S1]. Call it before any agent tracing calls such as `start_conversation()` or `start_turn()`. Without it, those functions silently do nothing [S2].

**What to pass in Python:** the recommended form is a `"team/project"` string:

```python
import weave
weave.init("[YOUR-TEAM]/[YOUR-PROJECT]")
```

- `[YOUR-TEAM]` is your CoreWeave Forge team name.
- `[YOUR-PROJECT]` is your Weights & Biases project name [S2].

You can also build the string, for example `weave.init(f"{TEAM}/{PROJECT}")` [S1].

**Bare project name:** other Python examples pass only a project name, such as `weave.init("langchain_demo")`. The LangChain page says this argument is a project name Weave uses to organize your traces [S4]. The TypeScript reference says the argument can be `project` or `entity/project`. If you omit the team, your default entity is used [S3]. I didn't find a Python reference page for `weave.init` in the snapshot, so I can't confirm that the Python default-entity behavior is identical. To avoid ambiguity, pass `team/project` explicitly.

**Next step:** put `weave.init("your-team/your-project")` near the top of your script, before you create any traces. Make sure `WANDB_API_KEY` is set in your environment. The quickstart does this before calling `weave.init` [S1].
